description: Explicit enforcement surface for every tracked script under scripts/, at any depth, with a .sh, .rb or .mjs extension. Verified by scripts/qa/test-qa-gate-surface.sh, which runs in the ci.yml governance job. A script on disk that is absent here fails the gate; so does an entry whose script no longer exists; and so does a script any workflow job runs that is declared neither as a gate in scripts[] nor as a non-gate in supportFiles[]. FR-147 added the third direction: the first two are satisfied by a manifest that has never heard of scripts/qa-doc-lint.sh, which ci.yml had been running for months while every scanner deriving its scope from this file read the gate that script invokes and skipped the script itself. FR-158 widened the first direction from scripts/qa to scripts, which brought in 28 files — among them all twelve shared libraries under scripts/lib that the ci-required gates source. Until then the gates were governed and the engine they run on was not, and a defect in a library reaches every caller at once.

enforcementKinds.ci-required: Executed by a GitHub Actions workflow on every push/PR. Requires workflow, job, and providerIsolation. Must never be able to reach a real provider binary.
enforcementKinds.manual-runbook: Executed by a human following the owner QA document. Requires reason and owner.
enforcementKinds.scheduled: Executed by a scheduled workflow, not on push/PR. Requires reason and owner in addition to workflow and job.

providerIsolationModes.no-provider: The script never applies a manifest bundle that declares an unpinned claude/codex agent driver.
providerIsolationModes.fixture-pinned: Every claude/codex agent in the named fixture bundle also declares binary: fake-*.
providerIsolationModes.path-shadow: The script copies a fake provider into an isolated bin directory and prepends it to PATH before starting a daemon.

supportFileRoles.fixture: Input data or a fake executable consumed by a gate. Never invoked as a gate itself, so it has no enforcement of its own.
supportFileRoles.library: Shared shell, ruby or node sourced or invoked by one or more gates. Runs only inside its callers, so it inherits their enforcement. This is where the gates' own engine lives — scripts/lib/rust_source.rb and workflow_model.rb decide what four ledgers count and what the workflow checks can see — so a defect here reaches every caller at once, which is the argument for classifying it rather than leaving it outside the scanned root.
supportFileRoles.release-tooling: Executed directly by a release workflow to build or publish an artifact, not to assert a governance property. Has no enforcement of its own because it makes no claim. Only valid for a script whose every executing workflow is tag- or dispatch-triggered: check_workflow_execution_declared rejects the role the moment such a script appears in a job of a workflow that runs on a branch push or a pull request, so this is not a place to park a governance gate.
supportFileRoles.generator: Executed directly by a workflow to produce an artifact, like release-tooling, but from a workflow that development activity can trigger — so the trigger rule that disciplines release-tooling cannot apply. What disciplines this role instead is `verifiedBy`: the entry must name a ci-required gate that regenerates the same artifact and compares, and check_workflow_execution_declared rejects the role if that gate is absent from this manifest or is not ci-required. The claim is therefore not 'this script is trustworthy' but 'something on every push proves its output'. Without that field the role would be release-tooling with its one condition removed, which is the amnesty §4.4 shape 8 describes.
supportFileRoles.developer-tool: Run by a person at a terminal, never by a workflow and never by a gate. It asserts nothing about this repository's invariants, so there is no enforcement claim to make and a break shows up the next time someone runs it. Distinct from manual-runbook, which is a gate a human executes against a written procedure and whose freshness is tracked; these have no procedure and no claim. Not a parking space for a gate: anything that checks an invariant belongs in .scripts[] with an enforcement.
supportFileRoles.spike: Throwaway prototype kept for the record, executed by nothing. It is not maintained, not run, and makes no claim; it is declared only so that it is visible to this manifest rather than sitting in an unscanned subtree. Declared per path — scripts/spikes is deliberately not a subtree exemption, because a directory-level ignore would go on absorbing files nobody has written yet and would never produce a line in any log.

commandSources.runnerBaselineReason: Present on both ubuntu-latest and macos-latest runner images. This is the one input that cannot be derived from the repository, so it is declared — and deliberately minimal: anything a job could plausibly need to install is left out, which makes the check strict rather than permissive. ripgrep is absent from both images and is exactly what this list must not paper over.

No exemption for a file that does not enable pipefail itself: shell options are dynamic, and run-cli-probes.sh sources every scenario into a shell that sets it. The reader leaves on the first match, the producer dies of EPIPE, and pipefail makes that the pipeline's answer - so a successful match reports as a failed one, or, where the match feeds the failing branch, a violation reports as clean (FR-145). Layer 4 of the self-bootstrap survival mechanism: it polls the binary on disk, health-checks it with `--help`, and copies the .stable snapshot back after WATCHDOG_MAX_FAILURES consecutive failures. It runs as an unbounded foreground loop that overwrites target/release/orchestratord, so no CI job can execute it; the runbook drives it with a two-second poll against a deliberately corrupted binary. Classified here rather than as a developer-tool because it does make a claim — that a corrupt build is repaired — and QA self-bootstrap/02 is the procedure that checks it.
